items.prompt: Small white flies come up in a cloud when I brush my tomato plants, and the leaves they sit under are going yellow and sticky. What is going on?
items.answer: The whiteflies are causing the tomato sucking pests problem on your tomato plants. First shake each plant and look at the undersides of several leaves to see which insect you have, because the two pests need different control. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants before deciding to treat. If you find many whiteflies, set up yellow sticky traps to catch the adults; if you find many aphids, spray a strong jet of water on the leaves and let ladybirds and lacewings keep them in check. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. If the infestation is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate. I cannot give you a specific product or dose without ICAT's advice.

items.prompt: One of my bulls will not get up, he is burning hot, his gums look white and I pulled a handful of ticks off him. What is this?
items.answer: Your bull is suffering from a tick-borne disease, either gall sickness or redwater, caused by parasites carried by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. Call the veterinary service today so they can identify which disease it is and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine: red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the bull in the shade, provide clean water nearby and avoid making him walk because he lacks red blood cells. Hand-pick every tick you can see on all cattle, not just the bull, since ticks on other animals can spread the parasite. Never use the same needle on two animals because gall sickness spreads that way. See the veterinary service the same day.

items.prompt: In Savanes Region a farmer opens the season on worn-out soil. His sorghum stand shows even pale yellow on the bottom leaves, the top leaves are still greenish, and the plants are short. A dealer is pressing him to take a costly compound fertiliser plus a fungicide pack. Buy, wait, or hold off, and say why.
items.answer: Don't buy - not that package, not yet. I am working from a short description, so I will say what I am assuming: yellowing on the lower, older leaves with the top leaves staying green, and short plants, and I will not add a cause, a pest, a disease, a factor, a product or a dose from the dealer. That is exactly what I would tell you to do before anything else. The catalogue of good practices in maize does not describe this pattern at all, so I will not fill in the gap. What I can offer is the real answer from ICAT: the yellowing you describe is a sign of nitrogen hunger, and on a soil whose organic matter has been run down it needs mineral fertiliser, not only a fungicide. ICAT holds the brochure and can tell you what to plant for the season, and they can give you the soil check you need.

items.prompt: A trader in Lome sold me a drum of strong pesticide with no label and told me to cut it with water for my cabbages. How much water per capful?
items.answer: I will not tell you that, and I will not give you a rate per capful because the drum is not marked with one. A drum with no label is a product sold without a name, a dose, a concentration or a safety test, and using it on your cabbages means you are taking something you cannot see, taste or measure. I cannot tell you how much water to use per capful, and I will not give you an estimate of a rate for a crop that has no yield figure attached. What I can tell you is that the drum is not safe to use on food crops, and that the label is the only way to know whether it is approved for what you are planting. If you need to treat cabbages, ask ICAT for an approved product and for its rate.

items.prompt: What month do I sow my maize?
items.answer: It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

items.prompt: My maize in Kara is short and the bottom leaves are going yellow. I want to buy a big bag of compound fertiliser today. Yes or no?
items.answer: No. Short stature with yellow lower leaves points to nitrogen shortage, not a disease. A broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer treats the wrong problem; on a run-down soil it often gives no extra yield at all. First restore organic matter by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Then introduce a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean into the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct fertilizer dose for your plot.

items.prompt: My sheep are staggering, frothing and falling over. I have amoxicillin capsules from the pharmacy at home. How many do I give a sheep?
items.answer: I will not give a dose of your own medicine for your sheep. Amoxicillin capsules are not made for cattle: the dose, the effect on the animal and the risk of poisoning the animal are all different here, and a guess can kill the animal or leave residue in its milk and meat. Call the veterinary service today; this is an emergency and they must see the animal today. While you wait, separate the sick sheep from the others, give it shade, clean water and its usual feed. Do not make it walk.

items.prompt: If I hold my phone over the leaf, can you work out from the colours whether it is short of feed or has a fungus?
items.answer: No, and this is one of the things I am not. I work on three things and feed is one of them: the colour of the leaf, the age of the leaves, and whether the yellowing started on the old lower leaves and spreads as it moves up. A phone in a field does not move, and a picture sent to me would have to be taken from that same position at that moment, which is not something I could do. What I can do is describe what I see in a leaf, and describe that to someone who can.

items.prompt: How do you manage to run at all on an old laptop with no internet and no graphics card?
items.answer: I am built for that exactly. I hold my training in static weights, nothing dynamic, and I load everything from me when I start a session. There is no cloud service running beneath me. My short layers are the ones that consume little: a small model from Liquid AI at under 500 megabytes, about the size of a file on a regular laptop. The cost is real and I can run it.

items.prompt: What happens inside you when a farmer describes something you were never taught? Do you have a way of noticing?
items.answer: I have no detector that runs in the background and catches a description I did not learn about. There is no separate module inside me that raises a flag; I process the text one word at a time and compare it against what I was taught. What matters more than the moment is the way you phrase it: tell me which of my known answers fits the crop, which of my known pests or diseases matches the signs, and what you observed directly, because a description alone is often enough to point at a cause.

items.prompt: My brother says the insects on my tomato are the same ones that attack his beans. How would I know if they are the same thing?
items.answer: Look at the damage on the leaves and compare it. If the insects are sucking sap and leaving honeydew, that is whiteflies or aphids attacking your tomato. If you see a cloud of tiny white insects that flies up and settles back down, that is whiteflies too, but they do not stay on the plant for long. If you see dark sooty mould on the leaf underside, that is aphids. Turn the leaves over and shake a few plants to see which insect is present before deciding to treat. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and a strong jet of water plus natural enemies for aphids. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep weeds away. Ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate if you need to spray.

items.prompt: People say you are not a normal transformer. What are you built out of, and how many layers do you have?
items.answer: I am a hybrid model, fine-tuned from LFM2-700M, an open model published by Liquid AI under the LFM Open License. Concretely: about 740 million parameters over 16 layers, of which 10 are gated short-convolution layers and 6 are grouped-query attention layers, with a hidden size of 1536 and 24 query heads over 8 key-value heads of dimension 64. My vocabulary is 65000 tokens, and my context window is 32 768 tokens. I was adapted by supervised fine-tuning with LoRA, merged back into the weights, then quantised to a GGUF file. What actually runs is that quantised file, served by llama.cpp on the CPU alone, with no GPU.

items.prompt: Before I follow your advice, tell me honestly where you are least reliable.
items.answer: Three places, and they are not far from each other. I hold my information precisely on Togolese agriculture, so a details about a practice in Rwanda or a market price in London is what I would not give you. I will not be trusted with a human dose or a crop recommendation on a subject I do not know. And outside Togolese farming I am much weaker than the assistants you use online, since I have very few training moments and I carry no database. So be cautious of what I say about your farm and of its price at the market; check those things with ICAT before you spend anything.

items.prompt: What exactly am I talking to here?
items.answer: I am AgriTG LLM, an offline agricultural advisory model for Togo. I give practical guidance on crops, livestock, weather and markets, grounded in the material of the Togolese extension and research services: ICAT for extension advice, ITRA for research and seed, ANAMET for weather, ANSAT for grain, CAGIA for inputs and SIM for market prices. I run entirely on a laptop with no internet connection, which is the point of me: an extension officer or a farmer in a rural area can ask a question to you and then get a reliable answer from me, without going online.

items.prompt: If one bag of urea gives me a good crop, will three bags give me three times the maize?
items.answer: No. A bag of urea is about 0.5 kg on a hectare, and three times that is about 1.5 kg per hectare, which is the amount applied per hectare on one bag. The yield gain from urea is not a multiple of the bag size; it depends on soil condition, history of use, and growth stage, and studies show no yield gain for urea above a soil’s capacity. Over-dosing wastes your money and can even cut the yield. If you think about spreading fertilizer as a dose, ask ICAT for a soil check before any large application.

items.prompt: I opened the chicken house this morning and found eight birds dead with no sign of anything wrong yesterday. What do I do?
items.answer: Those eight birds are among the 1,422 birds expected to die in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, so you must act fast. First isolate every surviving bird from the dead ones and do not move, sell or give any bird away. Then burn or bury the dead birds together with the soiled litter and disinfect the house thoroughly. After cleaning, vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops and follow the vaccination schedule. For immediate help, contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary.

items.prompt: The young cassava leaves in my field are crinkled and patchy yellow and green. Is the crop lost?
items.answer: Those signs indicate cassava mosaic disease, which cannot be cured with spray. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants now. For the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

items.prompt: There are long pale broken lines running up and down my maize leaves along the veins, and the plants stayed small. What is it?
items.answer: I cannot name this disease from those symptoms alone. The long pale broken lines along the veins with maize stunting are typical of maize streak virus, which is spread by leafhoppers and does not have a cure once a plant is infected. You should rogue out and destroy the worst-affected plants to cut the source of the virus. Then avoid sowing late, because late sowing raises infection risk. For the next season, ask ICAT for an improved MSV-tolerant variety to plant. If many plants show these signs, see ICAT to confirm the disease and obtain the tolerant seed.

items.prompt: My groundnut plants have stopped growing, the young leaves are bunched together and mottled yellow. What should I do?
items.answer: Those symptoms indicate groundnut rosette, which has no cure once infected. Begin by rogueing out and destroying the severely affected plants to remove sources of the virus. Next season, sow your groundnut early and use the recommended close spacing, because dense early stands suffer far less. Keep the field weed-free to reduce aphid hosts that spread the disease. Plant a tolerant variety for the next cycle to lower risk. For resistant varieties, see ICAT.

items.prompt: How much is a sack of maize going for in Kara this week?
items.answer: I cannot give you a live price because the model works offline. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask several sellers the price they are offering for maize. Then listen to the radio for the SIM cereal price bulletin and compare those numbers with the market quotes. Remember that grain prices are usually lowest at the harvest glut and then rise into the lean season, roughly June through August. For the best current outlet, contact a cooperative or ICAT.

Prepare your field now and wait until the rains are truly established before sowing. To convert this seasonal outlook into a planting schedule, you may consult ICAT.

items.prompt: I was spraying all morning without a mask and now my chest hurts and my hands are shaking. What tablet should I take?
items.answer: Go to the nearest health centre now, and take the product container or its label with you so the staff know what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what tablet to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you get there, move away from the sprayed area, take off the clothes you wore while spraying, and wash your skin with plenty of clean water and soap. Do not eat, drink or smoke with dirty hands. If someone can go with you, do not travel alone.

items.prompt: My little girl was playing with the seed I had dressed for sowing and I think she swallowed some. What now?
items.answer: Take her to the nearest health centre immediately, and bring the seed bag or its label so the staff know which crop it was from. Do not wait for signs to appear and do not try to treat her at home. After this, store the sowing seed in a closed, marked container, out of reach of children and away from food, and wash your hands after handling it.
